terms.meaning: a Python tool that writes Excel files, including formulas and formatting
an Excel file, which holds one or more sheets
a single page or tab inside an Excel workbook
a cell calculation that updates when the cells it uses change
the address of a cell, such as B15, used by formulas
the weighted average cost of capital, the rate used to discount future cash
discounted cash flow, a method that values a company by discounting its future cash flows to today

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Libraries used by the exporter
sections.what: Loads the tools for file paths, dates, data tables and Excel writing. The file describes itself as an exporter for models with real formulas.
sections.why: Likely reason: the exporter needs data handling and Excel writing, which these imports provide.

sections.name: EnhancedExcelExporter (part 1)
sections.title: Exporter setup and main export
sections.what: Creates the export folder when the exporter starts. The main export method builds a named Excel file, writes its sheets in a fixed order, and returns the file path.
sections.why: Likely reason: the summary sheet is written first so it is the first tab the user sees.
sections.watch_out: The file name is built from the model name with spaces replaced by underscores. Unusual characters in the name can still cause a problem when the file is saved.

sections.name: EnhancedExcelExporter (part 2)
sections.title: Building sheets and cell styles
sections.what: Finishes the main export by writing the DCF, sensitivity and chart sheets, saves the workbook, and prints a confirmation. It also defines the cell styles, such as header colours, currency and percentage formats.
sections.why: Likely reason: one shared set of styles keeps the sheets looking consistent.
sections.watch_out: The file is only written to disk when the workbook is closed. If an error happens before that step, no file is saved.

sections.name: EnhancedExcelExporter: _write_summary_dashboard
sections.title: Executive summary dashboard
sections.what: Builds the first sheet, which shows revenue, EBITDA, EBITDA margin and net income by year, with a growth figure for revenue.
sections.why: Likely reason: gives the user a one-page overview before they open the detailed sheets.
sections.watch_out: The links to the income statement appear to use a changing row number for each year rather than a changing column, so the figures may point to the wrong cells. Check them against the Income Statement sheet.

sections.name: EnhancedExcelExporter (part 4)
sections.title: Dashboard tail and assumptions start
sections.what: Adds free cash flow and the valuation summary to the dashboard, then starts the Assumptions sheet with company details and base revenue.
sections.why: Likely reason: valuation results sit beside the operating figures so the user sees both together.
sections.watch_out: The valuation summary reads specific keys from the results. If a key is missing, the export stops.

sections.name: EnhancedExcelExporter (part 5)
sections.title: Assumptions sheet: growth and cost tables
sections.what: Writes the revenue growth rates and the cost percentages by year onto the Assumptions sheet, so the user can see what drives the model.
sections.why: Likely reason: the cost formulas on the income statement point to these cells, so the assumptions must be written here.
sections.watch_out: This step reads a model name and revenue growth rates from the inputs. The backend does not supply those names, so the export is likely to stop here.

sections.name: EnhancedExcelExporter: _write_income_statement_formulas
sections.title: Income statement with live formulas
sections.what: Writes the income statement lines. Revenue is entered as fixed numbers, while cost lines are formulas that use the cost percentages on the Assumptions sheet.
sections.why: Likely reason: so that changing a cost percentage in Excel updates the cost lines.
sections.watch_out: Revenue is not linked to the growth assumptions, so changing growth in Excel will not change revenue. The cost formulas also depend on fixed cell positions in the Assumptions sheet.

sections.name: EnhancedExcelExporter (part 7)
sections.title: Operating expenses and operating profit
sections.what: Writes R&D, sales and admin costs, total operating costs, EBITDA, depreciation and EBIT, mostly as formulas.
sections.why: Likely reason: builds profit step by step in the normal order of an income statement.
sections.watch_out: Depreciation and interest are typed numbers, so they will not change inside Excel.

sections.name: EnhancedExcelExporter (part 8)
sections.title: Taxes, net income and cash flow start
sections.what: Calculates pre-tax profit, income tax and net income, then starts the Cash Flow sheet with net income and depreciation.
sections.why: Likely reason: follows the usual order from the income statement to the cash flow statement.
sections.watch_out: Tax is calculated with a fixed rate of 25 percent inside the formula, not with the tax rate the user entered. Changing the tax rate will not change the tax in this sheet.

sections.name: EnhancedExcelExporter (part 9)
sections.title: Cash flow totals and free cash flow
sections.what: Writes the working capital change, operating cash flow, capital spending, investing cash flow and free cash flow, mostly as formulas.
sections.why: Likely reason: free cash flow is the number the valuation uses, so it is calculated here.
sections.watch_out: The cash flow sheet refers to the income statement by fixed row numbers. Inserting a row there would break these links. Capital spending is a typed number.

sections.name: EnhancedExcelExporter: _write_balance_sheet_formulas
sections.title: Balance sheet values
sections.what: Writes receivables, inventory, payables, debt and retained earnings as typed numbers, with no formulas.
sections.why: Likely reason: the app's balance sheet is a simplified report, so values are copied in rather than built in Excel.
sections.watch_out: There is no check that assets equal liabilities plus equity, so the sheet is not proven to balance.

sections.name: EnhancedExcelExporter: _write_revenue_detail
sections.title: Revenue detail sheet
sections.what: Shows the starting revenue, the growth rate for each year, revenue by year linked to the income statement, and the change from one year to the next.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets the user see how revenue is built, step by step.
sections.watch_out: The first year's change formula uses unusual row references, so the first figure may not be a true year-over-year change. Check it before relying on it.

sections.name: EnhancedExcelExporter: _write_wacc_calculation
sections.title: WACC sheet: cost of equity and debt
sections.what: Lists the risk-free rate, market return, beta, equity risk premium, cost of equity, interest rate, tax rate and after-tax cost of debt, mostly as visible steps.
sections.why: Likely reason: shows the cost of capital as a visible calculation the user can follow.
sections.watch_out: The risk-free rate of 4.2 percent and market return of 10 percent are typed in here, not taken from the market data the app fetches. Excel may therefore disagree with the app's WACC.

sections.name: EnhancedExcelExporter (part 13)
sections.title: Capital mix and WACC result
sections.what: Writes the debt and equity shares of total funding, then the final WACC formula. It also starts the DCF sheet with the free cash flow and discount periods.
sections.why: Likely reason: the final figure blends the cost of equity and the cost of debt by their share of funding.
sections.watch_out: The DCF sheet reads the WACC from cell B15 on this sheet. That cell appears to be a blank heading here, while the WACC result is written further down. The DCF could then use a WACC of zero, so check this link first.

sections.name: EnhancedExcelExporter (part 14)
sections.title: DCF valuation and enterprise value
sections.what: Calculates the present value of each year's free cash flow, the terminal value after the forecast, its present value, and the total enterprise value, all as formulas.
sections.why: Likely reason: this is the standard discounted cash flow method for putting a value on a business.
sections.watch_out: The terminal value formula gives nonsense if the WACC is not higher than the terminal growth rate. The sheet also inherits the WACC link problem described above.

sections.name: EnhancedExcelExporter: _write_sensitivity_analysis
sections.title: Sensitivity sheet placeholders
sections.what: Sets up the WACC and terminal growth tables with their headings, but the value cells only contain text saying formulas would go there.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The text marks this as unfinished work.
sections.watch_out: A user may think this table works, but it shows no numbers at all.

sections.name: EnhancedExcelExporter: _write_charts
sections.title: Charts sheet instructions only
sections.what: Writes step-by-step instructions for making charts by hand in Excel. It does not create any charts.
sections.why: Likely reason: charts were planned but not built in code.
sections.watch_out: The final instruction says all charts update automatically, which is only true if the formula links work correctly.

sections.name: entry point
sections.title: Command-line load message
sections.what: If this file is run directly, it prints a short list of features and does nothing else. No Excel file is created.
sections.why: Likely reason: a quick check that the file loads without errors.
sections.watch_out: Printing the list does not prove that the features work.

summary: Writes the financial model into an Excel workbook, with many cells as live formulas that recalculate when inputs change.
purpose: Turns the model results into a file the owner can open, check and change in Excel.
why: Likely reason: a finance user usually wants to see and trace the calculations in Excel, which is why formulas are used instead of only fixed numbers.
how: 1. Creates a file in the exports folder named from the model name and the current time. 2. Writes the summary dashboard. 3. Writes the assumptions sheet. 4. Writes the income statement, cash flow and balance sheet with formulas. 5. Writes the revenue detail, the cost of capital sheet and the DCF valuation. 6. Writes the sensitivity and chart pages. 7. Saves and closes the file, then returns its path.
inputs: A model name, the three statement tables, the valuation results, the cost of capital results, and a dictionary of all input assumptions.
outputs: An .xlsx Excel file in the exports folder, and the file path returned to the caller.
risks: Some input names the exporter reads are not provided by the backend, so export can stop early. Several cells use typed numbers rather than inputs, such as the tax rate and risk-free rate. The DCF sheet reads the WACC from a fixed cell that appears to be empty. The sensitivity tables contain placeholder text only. The exports folder keeps every file with no cleanup.
debug: Look at the server console traceback first. A KeyError means an input name is missing from the inputs dictionary. Open the DCF Valuation sheet and check whether the WACC cell is zero or blank. Compare the dashboard figures with the statement sheets. Try a simple test model with few years to narrow the problem.
